plain: Goldman Sachs's headline measure of client money: everything it manages for clients plus some assets it only advises on or holds as private bank deposits.
technical: Per the 10-K: institutional clients' assets, assets sourced through third-party distributors and high-net-worth assets managed on a discretionary basis, plus client assets with third-party managers, private bank deposits and fee-earning advisory relationships without discretion. Excludes self-directed brokerage assets. $4,097bn at 30 Sep 2026.
why_it_matters: Management fees are driven by average AUS, so every flow a client team wins or loses moves this number. Do not call it AUM: AUS is wider.

plain: AUS excluding cash-like liquidity products: alternatives, equity and fixed income.
technical: GS reports net flows and the client-channel split (Institutional, Wealth management, Third-party distributed) on long-term AUS only. $3,046bn at 30 Sep 2026.
why_it_matters: When GS says 'long-term fee-based net inflows' it means flows into these assets, which carry higher fees than liquidity products.

plain: Cash-like holdings: money market funds and private bank deposits.
technical: A GS AUS asset class. $1,051bn at 30 Sep 2026; average effective fee 13 bps for nine months 2026.
why_it_matters: Large balances and low fees, and flows can reverse quickly. The reported class mixes money market funds with private bank deposits, so it is not a clean measure of the Liquidity Solutions fund business.

plain: How the client reaches Goldman Sachs: directly as an institution, as one of GS's own wealth clients, or through another firm that distributes GS products.
technical: GS reports long-term AUS in three channels: Institutional ($1,245bn), Wealth management ($1,087bn) and Third-party distributed ($714bn) at 30 Sep 2026. Global only; no regional split.
why_it_matters: The Institutional and Third-party distributed channels correspond most closely to institutional and third-party wealth client teams, but GS does not map channels to teams and gives no UK or EMEA channel figure.

plain: Client assets that come to GS funds through other firms, such as banks, wealth managers and platforms, and not from GS's own wealth clients.
technical: One of three GS client channels for long-term AUS. $714bn at 30 Sep 2026, up from $526bn a year earlier; net inflows of $97bn in the first nine months of 2026, which include acquired ETF assets.
why_it_matters: This is the disclosure line closest to what a third-party wealth team works on, at global level only.

plain: The average yearly fee GS earned per unit of client assets, shown in basis points.
technical: Disclosed by asset class and excluding non-asset-based fees. 2025: alternatives 58 bps, equity 54 bps, fixed income 17 bps, liquidity products 14 bps, total 31 bps.
why_it_matters: Shows why product mix matters: moving a pound from equity to fixed income or liquidity lowers revenue even if the client stays. It is a firm-wide blend, not the price of any mandate.

plain: The AWM revenue line for fees charged on client assets and related services.
technical: Mostly asset-based fees on managed client assets, plus advisory, planning and brokerage fees for wealth clients. $11,538m in 2025, of which Asset management $4,990m and Wealth management $6,548m.
why_it_matters: The recurring fee line that asset gathering and retention feed. Recurring does not mean guaranteed: it moves with markets, flows and mix.

plain: Extra fees GS earns when a fund or account beats an agreed return or benchmark.
technical: A percentage of return or of excess return, recognised only when significant reversal is not probable. Includes 'overrides' on private equity and credit funds. $489m in 2025; $882m in the first nine months of 2026.
why_it_matters: Lumpy and tied to realisations, so it should not be treated like recurring management fees in a worked example.

plain: GS's word for its larger share of profits on a private fund once returns pass a threshold; commonly called carried interest.
technical: Defined in the 10-K as 'the increased share of the income and gains derived primarily from our private equity and credit funds when the return on a fund's investments over the life of the fund exceeds certain threshold returns'.
why_it_matters: Use GS's own term when discussing its disclosures; a client-side reader will usually say carried interest.

plain: Alternative assets GS controls or has commitments for but does not currently charge management fees on.
technical: Mainly balance-sheet investments, unfunded commitments (GS's own and clients' where fees are not charged on commitments), fund credit facilities and employee funds. $207bn at 31 Dec 2025 against alternative AUS of $420bn.
why_it_matters: Explains why a commitment a client signs today may not produce fee revenue until capital is drawn and invested.

plain: A client's promise to provide money to a private fund when the manager calls for it.
technical: GS reports commitments raised ($115bn in 2025) separately from AUS; some become fee-earning AUS only 'if and when the commitments are drawn and assets are invested'.
why_it_matters: Keeps a fundraising headline apart from funded, fee-paying assets.

plain: The Goldman Sachs reporting segment that contains both Asset Management and Wealth Management.
technical: One of three segments with Global Banking & Markets and Platform Solutions. Net revenues $16,679m in 2025 (28.6% of the firm), of which Asset management $6,784m and Wealth management $9,895m.
why_it_matters: When someone says asset management is about 30% of Goldman's revenue they are quoting AWM, which also includes private banking, lending and principal investments.

expansion: Advisory and outsourced chief investment officer accounts
plain: A GS reporting bucket that combines assets it advises on with assets where it acts as a client's outsourced investment office.
technical: From Q4 2025 OCIO assets are 'reported in aggregate with advisory accounts'. In alternatives these accounts averaged $112bn in 2025 at 17 bps, against 77 bps on funds and discretionary accounts.
why_it_matters: Shows OCIO-type relationships carry a lower fee rate per pound than fund products, and that GS publishes no standalone OCIO total.
